beauty noun

classical

pulchritūdō, pulchritūdinis f.

noun, third declension

Beauty of body, of things and of the mind: Cicero defines it as a fit shape of the limbs with a pleasing colour (Tusc. 4.31), and speaks of the beauty of virtue (Off. 2.37). Its two kinds, he says, are venustās, womanly grace, and dignitās, manly dignity (Off. 1.130).

Other words

  • fōrma, fōrmae f. — good looks, beauty

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Ov. Ars 2.113; Hor. Ep. 1.4.6: dī tibi fōrmam … dederant (Lewis & Short)

    First shape, form, a figure (see form); used alone, a fine form, beauty, above all of a person.

  • venustās, venustātis f. — charm, grace, attractiveness

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.130 (Lewis & Short); Cic. Verr. 2.4.5: signa eximiā venustāte (Lewis & Short)

    Loveliness and grace, of people, of works of art and of wit and style; for Cicero the womanly kind of beauty (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • fōrma bonum fragile est, quantumque accēdit ad annōs fit minor, et spatiō carpitur ipsa suō

    beauty is a fragile good: the more the years increase, the less it becomes, and it is worn away by its own spanOv. Ars 2.113–114

  • sī quis in caelum ascendisset nātūramque mundī et pulchritūdinem sīderum perspexisset, īnsuāvem illam admīrātiōnem eī fore

    if a man went up to heaven and looked on the nature of the world and the beauty of the stars, the wonder of it would give him no joyCic. Amic. 88

  • Neque enim terrās tibi sed fōrmam aliquam ad eximiam pulchritūdinem pictam vidēberis cernere

    for you will think you are looking not at land but at a picture painted to be supremely beautifulPlin. Ep. 5.6.13

See also pretty, attractive, form, mole.
